sentences.text: The only valid species in the genus is Lesothosaurus diagnosticus.
This lightly built, bipedal animal ranged from 1 to 2 meters in length.
Its eye sockets were large, accounting for 36% of the skull's basal length.
Lesothosaurus had 15 to 16 tooth positions in its upper jaw, whereas the related Pisanosaurus had only 11 preserved.
The animal had only nine cervical vertebrae, though no complete neck series has been preserved.
Evidence of rapid tooth replacement has been found in the back teeth of Lesothosaurus.
Preserved ossified tendons on the back vertebrae suggest Lesothosaurus used them to counteract stress during bipedal movement.
The genus Lesothosaurus was named by paleontologist Peter Galton in 1978.
Fossils referable to Lesothosaurus may have been known as early as 1959.
Lesothosaurus fossils are found in the red and white sandstones and mudstones of the Upper Elliot and Clarens Formations.
Lesothosaurus likely was a fast runner due to its long slender legs and slender tail.
Lesothosaurus was likely an opportunistic omnivore that fed primarily on small animals when softer plants were unavailable.
Lesothosaurus sliced its food with its beak but could not chew it.
Evidence from a 2016 bonebed suggests Lesothosaurus may have lived in groups.
Researchers suggest that high diversity among heterodontosaurids, including Lesothosaurus, indicates species partitioned food sources to avoid competition.
A 1991 redescription by Paul Sereno classified Lesothosaurus as a basal member of the order Ornithischia.

Later studies placed Lesothosaurus as the most basal member of Neornithischia, relating it to Agilisaurus, Hexinulsaurus, and Nanosaurus, though some researchers debate whether it belongs to Neornithischia or is instead an early thyreophoran related to armored dinosaurs.
The Paleobi Database lists the parent group of Lesothosaurus as Thyreophora.
Lesothosaurus lived during the Early Jurassic period.
The fossils date to approximately 199 to 190 million years ago, specifically the Hettangian and Sinemurian ages.
It is debated whether Stormbergia is a valid species or a synonym of Lesothosaurus.
